claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy can exist as a single-phase FCC polycrystal after processing.
The relevant equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets can also be prepared as single-phase FCC alloys with comparable grain sizes and processing histories.
The controlled comparison should remove one or two elements from the quinary alloy while preserving FCC phase, grain size, processing history, test temperature, and strain rate.
Having a fifth constituent increases local lattice distortion in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni relative to its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Having a fifth constituent enhances chemical short-range order in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni relative to its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Atomic-size and modulus mismatches generate local stress-field fluctuations and severe lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion and local chemical heterogeneity produce rugged or stepped dislocation paths, variable dissociation widths, and local depinning events.
Chemical short-range order increases resistance to dislocation slip.
Short-range order slightly increases yield strength but does not necessarily change which plastic mechanisms are activated.
Greater lattice distortion and short-range order require higher stresses to sustain dislocation glide.
Quaternary and ternary subsets have less lattice distortion and weaker short-range order simply because they contain fewer constituents.
The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has higher yield strength than its equiatomic quaternary and ternary FCC subsets.
The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has a more pronounced work-hardening response than its equiatomic quaternary and ternary FCC subsets.
Quaternary and ternary subsets should show smoother dislocation glide and fewer pinned dislocation segments than the quinary alloy.
The predicted constituent-count effect applies only while phase constitution, grain size, processing history, strain rate, and test temperature are controlled.
Extreme test temperatures may obscure lattice-distortion effects because deformation is thermally activated.
Changes in stacking-fault energy may also contribute to differences in mechanical response.
A statistically insignificant difference in yield strength, work hardening, and correlated dislocation impediment between the quinary and lower-order alloys would falsify the hypothesis.
